procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 17.12.2020 passed by the Special Court rejecting the default bail application.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed an appeal before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana against the order of the Special Court. On 26.04.2022, the High Court dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 1011 of 2023 and Criminal Appeal No. 1012 of 2023 challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court heard both appeals analogously and dismissed them.

issue.issue_text: Whether cognizance of the chargesheet is necessary to prevent the accused from seeking default bail or whether mere filing of the chargesheet is sufficient.

facts: The issue before the court was whether an accused's right to default bail under Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) is extinguished by the mere filing of a chargesheet within the statutory period, or if the court must also take cognizance of that chargesheet within the same period.
law: The Court relied on its previous decision in *Suresh Kumar Bhikamchand Jain*.
Section 167 of the CrPC provides for the right to default (or statutory) bail if the investigation is not completed and a chargesheet is not filed within the prescribed time limit.
The scheme of the CrPC distinguishes between the investigation stage (governed by Section 167) and the post-cognizance/trial stage.
application: The Court clarified that the filing of a chargesheet is sufficient compliance with the requirements of Section 167 CrPC.
It reasoned that the purpose of Section 167 is to ensure the investigation is completed within a specific timeframe. The filing of the chargesheet marks the completion of this stage.
The act of taking cognizance is a separate judicial function that follows the investigation and is not relevant for the purpose of determining the right to default bail under Section 167.

Once the chargesheet is filed within the stipulated period, the accused's indefeasible right to be released on default bail comes to an end. The accused then remains in the custody of the Magistrate until the trial court takes cognizance and assumes custody for the purposes of the trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the mere filing of a chargesheet within the statutory period is sufficient to prevent an accused from seeking default bail. It is not necessary for the court to have taken cognizance of the chargesheet for this purpose.

issue.issue_text: The exclusion or inclusion of the date of remand for computation of the period prescribed under Section 167.

facts: An issue arose in a separate case (Criminal Appeal Nos. 701-702 of 2020) concerning whether the date of an accused's remand should be included or excluded when calculating the 60 or 90-day period for default bail under Section 167 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).
Due to a "divergence of opinions" on this specific point, the Court in that separate case referred the issue to be decided by a larger bench.
law: Section 167 of the CrPC prescribes the maximum period (typically 60 or 90 days) that an accused person can be detained in custody during an investigation before they become entitled to "default bail" if a charge-sheet is not filed.
application: The Court in the present case acknowledged that the specific question of how to compute the remand period is already pending before a larger bench.
The text explicitly states that the reference to the larger bench pertains to the issue of "exclusion or inclusion of the date of remand for computation of the period prescribed under Section 167."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue on its merits in this particular case. Instead, it concluded that since the exact same question was already referred to and pending before a larger bench in another matter, there was no need to make another reference from the current case. Therefore, the court rejected the request to refer this case to a larger bench on that issue.

cases.case_name: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India and Others
cases.principle: An offence is to be tried exclusively by the Special Court set up under the relevant Act, and in the absence of any Special Court, then by the Court of Sessions alone.

cases.case_name: Suresh Kumar Bhikamchand Jain v. State of Maharashtra and Another
cases.principle: Regarding the application of Section 167 of the Code in relation to a case involving an offence punishable under the Act, subject to certain modifications.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 45 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) must be read in conjunction with Rules 3 and 4 of the 2008 Rules.
obiter: It is not necessary for the court to discuss every decision relied upon by counsel, especially when those decisions are based on the peculiar facts of their respective cases and are not of any assistance to the appellant.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court dismissed the appeals, concluding that the case law relied upon by the appellants was not applicable to the present matter. The court found that each of the decisions cited by the appellants was rendered based on the peculiar facts of that specific case and, therefore, was of no assistance to the appellants' arguments.
legal_tests_applied: When evaluating a sanction order, 'the court has to find out whether there has been an application of mind on the part of the sanctioning authority concerned on the material placed before it. It is so necessary for the reason that there is an obligation on the sanctioning authority to discharge its duty to give or withhold sanction only after having full knowledge of the material facts of the case.'
why_appellant_lost: The case law relied upon by the appellants was found to be of no avail, as the court determined that 'Each of the decisions are in the peculiar facts of the case' and thus not applicable.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded because the court rejected the legal precedents cited by the appellants as being factually distinguishable and therefore not persuasive in the context of the current appeals.
policy_considerations: The debate on Section 167 must also be looked at from the perspective of expeditious conclusion of investigation and from the angle of personal liberty.
The right of default bail is an indefeasible right which cannot be allowed to be frustrated by the prosecution.
The provisions in regard to the sanction must be observed with complete strictness keeping in mind the public interest and the protection available to the accused against whom the sanction is sought.
